claims.text: No single number measures a country's development, so a variety of indicators is used together: GNI per head (a country's total yearly income divided by its population) for the economic side, and birth rate, life expectancy (the average number of years a newborn can expect to live), infant mortality (the number of children per 1000 who die before their first birthday) and the literacy rate for the social side, with access to safe water and the number of doctors per 1000 people also used; the indicators usually move together, which is why several read together give a fairer picture than one alone.

claims.text: Norway and Niger sit at opposite ends of the indicator tables (approximate figures, around 2022): life expectancy about 83 years in Norway against about 62 years in Niger; infant mortality about 2 deaths per 1000 live births in Norway against about 60 per 1000 in Niger; Norway's GNI per head many times Niger's; and a literacy rate close to full in Norway while roughly one adult in three can read and write in Niger.

claims.text: Describing development from a resource needs the pattern stated in words and each statement supported with a figure from the resource, with its unit; quoting statistics alone, or giving words alone, are the two common errors. The test is whether there is a statement and a figure that backs it.

claims.text: Infant mortality is the number of children per 1000 live births who die before their first birthday; it falls as health care, nutrition and clean water improve, so a falling infant mortality rate is a sign of rising development.

claims.text: Development is uneven between countries: north-west Europe, North America and parts of east Asia sit near the top of most indicator tables, while much of sub-Saharan Africa and parts of south Asia sit near the bottom, and the gap in GNI per head between the richest and poorest countries is wide.

claims.text: The reasons countries stay less developed act together: physical barriers such as deserts and a landlocked position raise the cost of trade; a colonial history often left single-crop economies; diseases such as malaria burden hot, wet regions; political instability and war deter investment; and debt repayments can swallow money that would otherwise fund schools and health care.

claims.text: A trend question is answered by stating the overall trend first (rising, falling, a widening or narrowing gap), then supporting figures and any exception; comparing two individual years without a statement of what the whole series does is the common error. The test is whether the answer says in one sentence what the whole table shows.

claims.text: Inequality also exists within countries. Namibia shows it: jobs and services concentrate in Windhoek and the coastal Erongo region around Swakopmund and Walvis Bay, while the north-eastern regions such as Kavango East and Zambezi record the highest poverty rates (2015/16 survey pattern), and income distribution as a whole is among the most unequal in the world, with a Gini coefficient around 0.56 (2015/16 figure).

claims.text: Production is classified into four sectors: the primary sector extracts raw materials (farming, fishing, mining, forestry); the secondary sector manufactures or processes goods (a cement works, a cannery, a weaving mill); the tertiary sector provides services (teaching, nursing, transport, banking, shop work); and the quaternary sector covers research, information and development, such as software engineering. The test for a job is what it does with the material, not the material itself.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The same material passes through the sectors: cotton is grown in the primary sector, spun and woven in the secondary, sold in a shop in the tertiary, and a firm breeding a better seed variety works in the quaternary - so classifying means asking what the job does with the material.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Employment structure - the share of workers in each sector - shifts with development. In low-income countries most workers are in the primary sector, mainly farming; in middle-income countries the secondary share grows as investment builds factories; in high-income countries most workers are in the tertiary sector, with services expanding as incomes and education rise and a small quaternary sector appearing.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Employment structure records shares (per cent of workers in each sector), not numbers of jobs: a country with a large population can hold more farmers in total than a small country while having a smaller share of them.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The primary share falls as a country develops because machines and better seed raise each farmer's output (so fewer farmers can feed the country), because better-paid secondary and tertiary jobs draw workers to towns, and because rising incomes create demand for services - the share falls even though output rises.

claims.text: Globalisation is the growing links between countries through trade, investment, communication and culture, driven by container shipping that cut the cost of carrying goods across oceans, by communications (the internet, mobile phones) that let a firm manage factories and suppliers on several continents at once, and by trade agreements and transnational corporations that move investment to where costs are lower and sell where markets are largest.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Globalisation can benefit low-income countries: transnational corporations build factories where labour costs less, so wages arrive where few formal jobs existed before; the same links open export markets to local producers; and imported goods cost consumers less than home-made equivalents, which raises living standards.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Globalisation can bring problems: production moves to wherever costs are lowest, so jobs can be lost in old industrial towns; a transnational corporation's profits flow to its headquarters country, so part of the wealth a host country creates leaves it; and dependence on one industry or export leaves places exposed when the links move on.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Weighing globalisation means stating a judgement and backing it with evidence, naming who gains and who loses: for many low-income countries the gain in jobs and export income is real, but the gains can be fragile, because the same links let production move on when wages or costs rise elsewhere - so the judgement usually lands on benefit with dependence.

claims.text: Shoprite Holdings, a transnational corporation (a company that operates in more than one country), grew from a Cape Town supermarket chain founded in 1979 into Africa's largest food retailer, with its head office at Brackenfell in Cape Town, a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, and by the 2020s more than 3 000 stores in about 15 African countries (approximate figures); Namibia was its first step outside South Africa in 1990, and it now trades from more than 30 Namibian towns.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Shoprite's global links run in both directions: goods are sourced from farms and factories in several countries and move through the group's large distribution centres in South Africa to Namibian shelves, though stores also buy from Namibian bakers, dairies and vegetable growers; Namibian staff work in the stores; and the money shoppers pay flows back partly as wages and local supplier payments and partly as profit to shareholders outside the country, because buying and pricing are decided at the Cape Town head office.

claims.text: Location reasons (the market is there, labour costs less, transport links, government incentives) are not the same as impacts (jobs created, wages paid, profits leaving the country): describing what a transnational corporation does in a place answers a different question from why it operates there. The test is whether the answer says why it is there, or what it does there.
